extraction.name: FLEURS
extraction.description: An n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau; Min Ma; Simran Khanuja; Yu Zhang; Vera Axelrod; Siddharth Dalmia; Jason Riesa; Clara Rivera; Ankur Bapna
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was built from FLoRes-101 dev and devtest sentences, split into new train/dev/test sets, and for each sentence in 102 languages three recordings were collected from three different native speakers, followed by validation by additional workers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Physical data collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: About 21.5% of the sentences are missing in the first version because none of the three recordings were validated.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Sentences from the FLoRes-101 dataset extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages, plus collected speech recordings for each sentence.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The text was tokenized and normalized by applying NFC and FST normalization, lowercasing, normalizing and removing punctuation, and splitting words into characters; three transcript versions are provided: raw, normalized, and character-based.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each recording was evaluated by additional workers to determine whether it corresponded to the input sentence, and invalid recordings were discarded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Invalid recordings were discarded after worker evaluation, leaving between zero and three recordings per sentence.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers; balance in terms of sex ratio of at least 30/70%, when possible.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to fill missing gaps in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding, with the hope of building speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset imposes a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible, and performance differences across geographical groups may reflect unequal amounts of available pre-training data.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: About 21.5% of sentences are missing in the first version because none of the three recordings were validated; training from scratch on FLEURS will easily overfit; and there are performance degradations for unseen languages and some language groups.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset can be used for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation, Retrieval, Speech-to-Text and Speech-to-Speech Translation, and multilingual speech-text retrieval; it is intended as an evaluation benchmark and supports train/dev/test splits.

name.evidence: We introduce FLEURS, the Few-shot Leaming Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech benchmark.

description.evidence: FLEURS is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Our data collection process is simple. We start with the FLoRes101 dataset. FLoRes-101 contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and these sentences have been translated in 101 languages by human translators. Because the test set of FLoRes-101 is not publicly available, we only use the dev and devtest sets, which contain 2009 sentences in total. We split those sentences into new train, dev and test splits, with 1509, 150 and 350 sentences respectively. For each sentence in the 102 languages (101 counted in FLoRes plus English, see Table 9), we collected three recordings by three different native speakers, imposing a balance in terms of sex ratio of at least 30/70%, when possible. After this first recording step, each recording is evaluated by additional workers to assesses whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To ease the pain for other researchers and facilitate apple-to-apple comparisons and reproducibility, we provide the tokenized versions of the sentences. We apply NFC and then FST normalization to each sentence, lower-case, normalize and remove punctuations. We also split words into characters, and define the token jas word boundaries. For each sentence, three versions are provided: the original raw transcript ( SRC RAW ), the preprocessed version ( SRC NORM ) and its character-based version ( SRC CHAR ), which should be used for ASR.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding. We hope this dataset will catalyze research in few-shot understanding in many languages, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: For each sentence in the 102 languages (101 counted in FLoRes plus English, see Table 9), we collected three recordings by three different native speakers, imposing a balance in terms of sex ratio of at least 30/70%, when possible. We observe in Table 4 that results are much better on the Westem European group (with 10.7 and 10.6 average CER) than on other groups like Sub-Saharan African (15.6 and 16.4 average CER) or South Asian (17.4 and 19.2), which can be explained in part due to the larger amounts of unlabeled data in WE languages from MLS and V oxPopuli.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. Training a giant model from scratch on the FLEURS dataset will easily overfit. For languages which were not seen in pre-training, a large fraction observed a test CER worse than global average due to fine-tuning on very limited amount of supervised data.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: FLEURS can be used for a variety of speech tasks, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation and Retrieval. FLEURS is well-suited for several downstream tasks including ASR, Speech-to-Text and Speech-to-Speech Translation, Speech LangID, and Multilingual Speech-to-Speech and Speech-to-Text Retrieval.
